title: Acute Lassa Virus Encephalitis with Lassa Virus in the Cerebrospinal Fluid but Absent in the Blood: A Case Report with a Positive Outcome
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old woman from Ekpoma, Edo State, Nigeria, presented with 4 days of high-grade fever, chills, and headache. She had no sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, mucosal bleeding, neck pain, or neck stiffness. Six months earlier she had cared for her twin sister, who had a prolonged febrile illness complicated by acute sensorineural deafness. At presentation, temperature was 39.5 °C, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, pulse 96 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 /min. A blood smear showed scanty Plasmodium falciparum; serum RT-PCR for Lassa virus was negative. Blood cultures remained sterile. Physical examination was unremarkable except for two 1 × 1.5 cm right submandibular lymph nodes. She was treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole. Eight days later she was discharged at her request on oral quinine, doxycycline, and cefuroxime, after repeat malaria smear was negative but fever persisted.

Two days after discharge, she was readmitted with irrational behavior at home, persistent high fever, and increasing confusion. On readmission, temperature was 38.4 °C, pulse 96 bpm, blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 24 /min. There were no signs of meningeal irritation, but she was irritable, confused, and aphasic. A clinical diagnosis of acute viral encephalitis was made. On the first day of readmission, serum RT-PCR for Lassa virus was again negative. The next day, blood was sent for Lassa virus IgM and IgG serology, and a lumbar puncture was performed. CSF showed 300 cells/mm³ (20% neutrophils, 80% lymphocytes), protein 35 mg/dL, glucose 55 mg/dL (59% of simultaneous blood glucose 93 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative and culture sterile. Serum liver-function tests were elevated; serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and hemoglobin were normal. Urinalysis showed 3+ proteinuria and 2+ microscopic hematuria. A PCR-based pan-flavivirus assay excluded Dengue and Yellow fever. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria considered given parasitemia and endemicity — “her blood film smear showed scanty Plasmodium falciparum…because malaria is a common cause of fever in our environment.”  
2. Septicemia considered; excluded by negative cultures — “blood culture performed 2 days later yielded no bacterial growth even after 7 days of incubation.”  
3. Bacterial meningitis considered; excluded by lack of meningeal signs and negative CSF studies — “there were no signs suggestive of meningeal irritation…Gram stain of the CSF was negative and the culture sterile.”  
4. Metabolic encephalopathy considered; excluded by normal metabolic panels — “the serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood sugar, and haemoglobin levels were normal, thus making encephalopathy from a metabolic cause an unlikely diagnosis.”  
5. Dengue and Yellow fever considered; excluded by pan-flavivirus PCR — “a PCR-based pan-flavivirus assay excluded Dengue and Yellow fever.”  
6. Lassa fever suspected clinically due to outbreak and exposure history — “LF was suspected because there was an outbreak in Ekpoma at the time.”  
7. Lassa fever confirmed by detection of virus in CSF despite negative serum RT-PCR — “an aliquot of the CSF sample was tested for the presence of LAV by the RT-PCR method: the result was positive.”
